item.title: ArborGold
item.description:
Arborists can build quotes from price lists, schedule crews, and send invoices from the field. Mobile apps let crews see jobs and update status. Customer history helps with repeat work and follow-ups.

It is aimed at small and mid-size companies. Features are practical rather than AI heavy.

Jobber and Housecall Pro are broader field service alternatives. ArborGold suits tree care businesses.

item.title: Floranext
item.description:
Designers take phone and web orders, print tickets, and schedule deliveries. Customer records track occasions for reminders. Online stores are built into the system.

It is a subscription product for flower shops.

Lightspeed and Shopify can work with extra setup. Floranext suits floral designers who run a shop.

item.title: Fresha
item.description:
Salons manage calendars, take payments, and send reminders. Clients find and book services on a marketplace. Reports track sales and staff performance.

The software is free to start, with fees on payments and some features.

Vagaro and StyleSeat are alternatives. Fresha suits cosmetologists and salon owners.

item.title: IBM Maximo
item.description:
It stores maintenance history for equipment, creates work orders, and tracks inspections. Add-on modules apply AI to predict failures, read inspection images, and monitor condition. Aviation operators use its aviation edition for aircraft maintenance records and task cards.

It is a heavy enterprise system that needs configuration and training. Smaller operations may find lighter tools easier.

SAP, Fiix, and UpKeep cover similar maintenance work. Maximo suits large maintenance organizations.

item.title: MassageBook
item.description:
Clients book and fill out intake forms online. Therapists record notes after each session and send reminders. A free plan covers basics, and paid plans add marketing tools.

It is built for solo practitioners and small clinics.

Vagaro and Jane are alternatives. MassageBook suits massage therapists.

item.title: Mindbody
item.description:
Studios set up classes, accept bookings, and manage memberships. Clients book through a branded app or the Mindbody marketplace. Reporting and marketing tools support growth, and AI features help with messaging.

It is a subscription product with tiered pricing.

Vagaro and Zen Planner are alternatives. Mindbody suits yoga instructors who run a studio.

item.title: MoeGo
item.description:
Groomers see appointments by staff and van, store pet profiles, and send reminders. Customers book online and pay by card. AI answers calls and messages in some plans.

It is a subscription product.

Gingr and Pawfinity are alternatives. MoeGo suits pet groomers and small pet service shops.

item.title: Passare
item.description:
Directors build arrangements, collect e-signatures, and share planning details with families. Obituary and tribute tools help families write remembrances. Reports track revenue and pre-need contracts.

It is a subscription product for funeral homes.

FrontRunner and Osiris are alternatives. Passare suits funeral directors.

item.title: Shopmonkey
item.description:
Technicians and service advisors build estimates from labor guides and parts catalogs, send them to customers for approval, and track the job through completion. Digital vehicle inspections with photos help explain recommended work. Text messaging keeps customers informed.

Shops use it to replace paper tickets and spreadsheets. Parts ordering and accounting integrations vary by plan.

Tekmetric and Shop-Ware are close alternatives. Shopmonkey suits independent repair shops.

item.title: Tekmetric
item.description:
Service advisors write estimates, send digital inspections with photos, and collect approval and payment by text or email. Reports show car count, average repair order, and technician productivity. Integrations connect to parts suppliers and accounting software.

Shops use the data to see what is working and where jobs stall. It is a subscription product with per-shop pricing.

Shopmonkey and Shop-Ware are alternatives. Tekmetric suits independent shop owners and managers.

item.title: Zen Planner
item.description:
Owners set up class schedules and membership plans, and members check in with an app or kiosk. Automated billing reduces missed payments. Reports show attendance and retention.

It is a subscription product.

Mindbody and Kicksite are alternatives. Zen Planner suits martial arts instructors who run a school.

item.title: Adobe Firefly AI Assistant
item.description: Firefly AI Assistant is Adobe’s attempt to bring an agent into its creative apps. Instead of opening each application and applying tools by hand, you describe an outcome, such as adapting a campaign image into several social formats or preparing a video with captions, and the assistant works out the steps. It then carries them out across the right apps in order. The project began under the name Project Moonlight before launching as Firefly AI Assistant.

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.description: AgentCore addresses the infrastructure work of taking an agent from prototype to production. A runtime hosts agents with session isolation so each user’s work is kept separate, and handles scaling. Identity features let agents authenticate to other services on a user’s behalf, a gateway turns existing APIs and services into tools agents can call, and observability traces what agents do. Developers can use it with frameworks such as LangGraph, CrewAI, and the Strands Agents SDK, and with models on Bedrock or from other providers.

item.title: Anaplan
item.description:
Anaplan lets large organizations plan in a connected way. Instead of separate spreadsheets for finance, sales, and operations, teams build models on a shared platform so a change in one area, such as a drop in demand, flows through to inventory, headcount, and budget. Its modeling engine handles large multidimensional data, and planners can create scenarios to see the effects of different decisions before committing.

AI features aim to lower the barrier to building and using models. An assistant can help create or modify model logic from natural language, forecast with machine learning, and summarize results for decision-makers. The platform integrates with ERP, CRM, and data warehouse systems to pull in actuals, and offers applications for common planning needs, such as sales territory planning and supply chain optimization.

item.title: Bland AI
item.description:
Bland provides voice agents that talk on real phone calls. Companies use them to answer inbound calls, call leads, confirm appointments, and run surveys, replacing or supplementing call center staff. The agents speak naturally, handle interruptions, and can work around the clock.

Developers control behavior through a system of Conversational Pathways, which define the steps and branches of a call, along with tools to call APIs, look up records, and update systems. The platform supports many languages and voices, call analytics, and handoff to human agents. It offers APIs for scaling to large volumes of calls.

item.title: Databricks Agent Bricks
item.description: Agent Bricks is aimed at companies that want agents grounded in their own data. Rather than writing everything by hand, a team describes the task, such as answering questions over internal documents, extracting information from forms, or coordinating several agents, and the platform helps build it. It generates synthetic test data, evaluates quality with judges, and tunes the agent by trying different models and settings to improve accuracy and cost.

item.title: Dropbox Sign
item.description:
Dropbox Sign lets people sign documents without printing them. You upload a file, mark where each signer needs to sign or fill in fields, and send it by email. Signers open it on any device, sign, and the finished copy is stored with an audit trail that shows who signed and when. Templates make repeat documents such as contracts and NDAs quick to send.

The product started as HelloSign and was acquired by Dropbox, which renamed it. It connects with Dropbox storage, Google Drive, Gmail, Microsoft tools, and CRM systems, so documents can be sent from where they already live. A developer API lets software companies embed signing flows inside their own products, and Dropbox has added AI features in its wider document tools.

item.title: Dynatrace
item.description:
Dynatrace is one of the established names in monitoring large, complex IT environments. A single agent, OneAgent, installs on servers, containers, and cloud services and automatically discovers applications and their dependencies, then collects metrics, traces, logs, and user experience data without much manual setup. A model of how components relate, kept up to date automatically, lets the platform see how a slowdown in one service affects others.

Its distinguishing feature is Davis AI. Instead of only alerting when thresholds are crossed, Davis uses causal analysis to identify the likely root cause of a problem and the business impact, reducing the pile of alerts into a smaller number of actionable issues. Newer generative AI features let users ask questions in natural language, and the platform adds automation that can trigger remediation. Dynatrace also covers security, application vulnerabilities, and monitoring of AI workloads.

item.title: Figma Weave
item.description: Weave brings generative image workflows into Figma. Instead of exporting an image to another tool, a designer can run a prebuilt workflow on a selected layer, for example swapping the background of a product shot, applying an artistic style to an image, or creating variations. More than twenty such workflows cover common creative tasks, and the results land back in the design file, ready to be used in a layout.

item.title: Gemini Code Assist
item.description:
Gemini Code Assist brings Google’s models into the developer’s editor. In VS Code and JetBrains IDEs, it suggests code as you type, answers questions in chat, explains and refactors code, generates tests, and helps fix errors. It can take a larger task and make coordinated changes across files in agent mode. Google also offers a command-line version, Gemini CLI, which many developers use directly in the terminal.

For organizations, enterprise editions add code customization, which lets the assistant take into account a company’s private repositories so its suggestions follow internal libraries and styles, as well as security and compliance features, indemnification, and admin controls. It works with Google Cloud tools such as Cloud Shell, Firebase, and BigQuery, and it can review pull requests on GitHub through a companion app.

item.title: GitHub Agent HQ
item.description: Agent HQ is GitHub’s way of treating coding agents as a team you manage instead of a single assistant. Rather than choosing one AI vendor, a developer can assign work to agents from different providers, such as OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code, from the same place where code, issues, and pull requests already live. Each agent works on its task and returns changes for review in the usual pull request flow.

item.title: HoneyBook
item.description:
HoneyBook is designed for people who sell services, such as photographers, designers, coaches, and consultants. A client inquiry arrives through a form, the owner sends a proposal with a contract and an invoice, and the client signs and pays online, all within a single flow. This replaces a patchwork of documents, email threads, and payment apps.

Other features support day-to-day work. Automations send reminders and follow-ups, a scheduler lets clients book meetings, and a client portal keeps messages, files, and payments in one timeline. Templates for proposals and questionnaires make repeat work faster, and AI helps draft emails and project descriptions. Reports show income and pipeline.

item.title: Housecall Pro
item.description:
Housecall Pro helps small service companies run their operations. Office staff schedule jobs and dispatch technicians on a calendar and map, customers receive confirmations and arrival notifications, and technicians use a mobile app to see their jobs, send estimates, collect signatures, and take payments on site. Invoices and payments flow into accounting.

The platform includes marketing and sales tools. Review requests, email campaigns, and a customer database help a business grow repeat work, and a booking widget lets homeowners schedule online. Some AI features answer calls and messages, help with scheduling and follow-ups, and summarize job details so owners can stay on top of the business.

item.title: IBM Bob
item.description:
Bob is IBM’s agentic assistant for software development. Instead of only autocompleting code, it takes part in the full lifecycle: understanding a codebase, planning changes, writing and reviewing code, generating tests, and helping with deployment. Different agents take on roles, such as architect or reviewer, and work inside the developer’s editor.

Enterprise use is the focus. IBM emphasizes security and governance, with protection against sensitive data leaks, policy enforcement, and testing of the AI for vulnerabilities. It routes tasks among several language models, including IBM’s own Granite family and models from other providers, and is positioned for modernization work such as moving older Java or COBOL applications.

item.title: Kore.ai
item.description:
Kore.ai helps large organizations deploy virtual assistants. Companies design conversations and workflows in a low-code environment, connect them to back-end systems, and publish them on websites, mobile apps, messaging platforms, and voice lines. The assistants can answer questions and complete tasks such as resetting a password or checking a balance.

The platform has moved from rule-based dialogue to generative AI and agents. It supports large language models from several providers, retrieval over company content, and tools for building multi-agent systems, with governance features for testing and monitoring. Prebuilt solutions for banking, healthcare, retail, and HR speed up projects, and agent assist tools support human staff on live calls.

item.title: Mistral Vibe
item.description:
Vibe is Mistral’s agent for software work. The command-line version runs in a project directory, reads and writes files, searches code, runs shell commands, and tracks tasks, using Mistral’s coding models to carry out requests such as fixing bugs, adding features, and explaining code. It is open source under the Apache 2.0 license, written in Python, and integrates with editors such as Zed and with other tools.

The broader Vibe offering extends agent capabilities to office tasks and teams. It builds on Mistral’s Devstral coding models and its large general models, which are available through Mistral’s API and, for some, as open weights that organizations can run on their own servers. This flexibility is a selling point for companies and governments that want agents without relying on US cloud providers.

item.title: NemoClaw
item.description:
OpenClaw is an open-source agent project that can carry out tasks on a user’s computer and accounts, which made it popular and also raised security worries. NemoClaw is NVIDIA’s response for organizations: it installs OpenClaw inside an isolated runtime, called OpenShell, with strict default permissions, so the agent can only touch what administrators allow. A privacy router helps decide which requests can use outside models and which stay local.

NVIDIA pairs the platform with its Nemotron models and with its NeMo software for building and managing agents, but says NemoClaw works on different hardware and with other models. It was announced with a group of enterprise partners and early integrations with agent frameworks, positioning NVIDIA to offer software as well as chips for the agent era.

item.title: Notion Custom Agents
item.description: Custom Agents extend Notion AI from something you chat with into something that works on its own. A team sets up an agent with instructions and the content it can access, then chooses what should trigger it: a schedule, a comment on a page, a change to a database, an @mention, or messages in a public Slack channel. The agent then does the job, such as triaging incoming requests, compiling a weekly report, updating a tracker, or answering questions in a channel.

item.title: Perplexity Computer
item.description: Perplexity Computer extends Perplexity from answering questions to doing work. You give it a goal, such as researching a market and building a report, tracking a set of sources, or assembling a presentation, and it plans the job, splits it into parts, and runs them, sometimes in parallel. Different steps are sent to different AI models depending on what they are good at, which is the central idea of the product.

item.title: Replit Agent 4
item.description: Replit Agent 4 continues the idea that you can describe software and have an agent build it. In the Replit workspace, you explain what you want, and the agent writes the code, sets up the environment and database, tests the result, and deploys it. You review progress, give feedback in plain language, and ask for changes. Replit says this version is substantially faster than its predecessor, which matters because building an app involves many steps.

item.title: Salesforce Agentforce
item.description: Agentforce lets companies deploy AI agents that work inside Salesforce. An agent might answer customer questions, qualify inbound leads, schedule meetings, or update records, using the company’s own data and rules. Builders define an agent’s role, topics, and the actions it may take, connect it to knowledge and data, and test it before release. A reasoning engine decides how to handle each request, and guardrails limit what the agent may do.

item.title: SAP Concur
item.description:
Concur is a staple of corporate finance. Employees book travel, capture receipts with a phone, and submit expense reports, which flow through approvals and into accounting systems. Policies are applied automatically, flagging out-of-policy spending, and credit card feeds reduce manual entry. Finance teams use it to control costs, reimburse employees, and meet audit requirements.

The platform has grown to include invoice and travel management, with integrations to airlines, hotels, and payment providers. AI supports automatic receipt reading, categorization, audit of expenses to detect errors or fraud, and assistance through SAP’s Joule for answering questions and completing tasks. Reporting provides visibility into travel and spending trends.

item.title: SAP Joule
item.description:
Joule is the assistant inside SAP’s software. Instead of navigating menus in an ERP, finance, or HR system, users ask questions such as which invoices are overdue or what the status of an order is, and Joule retrieves the answer from live business data. It respects the user’s permissions, so it only shows what that person is allowed to see.

It has grown from a question-and-answer helper into a platform for agents. Prebuilt Joule agents handle tasks like processing invoices or supporting recruiters, and Joule Studio lets customers and partners build their own agents and skills that work across SAP and non-SAP systems. SAP presents this as part of a broader business AI platform that connects data and models.

item.title: ServiceNow Otto
item.description:
Otto is ServiceNow’s way of unifying its AI products into a single assistant. It combines the conversational search that came from Moveworks, the workflow skills of Now Assist, and an agentic interface on the Now Platform. An employee can ask for help in plain language, and Otto finds an answer or starts the workflow that does the job, such as requesting access or opening an IT ticket.

The point is action across systems. ServiceNow positions it as an assistant that works with the enterprise tools a person already uses, not just answering from a knowledge base. Governance is a major theme: AI Control Tower tracks the agents, logs interactions, and enforces policies, which matters when many agents are acting at once.

item.title: Slackbot
item.description:
Slackbot used to be a simple helper that answered canned questions. It has been rebuilt as an agent that works across a Slack workspace. You can ask it to find a decision made in a channel, summarize a thread, draft a message or a document, schedule a meeting from calendar availability, or pull together information from several conversations, and it answers using content you already have permission to see.

Beyond answering, it can take actions. Slackbot can post, set reminders, update records through connected apps, and delegate longer tasks to agents built with Salesforce’s Agentforce, tying Slack more closely to the rest of Salesforce’s platform. Slack has used models from partners to power it, and the assistant adapts to the user’s context and role within the workspace.

item.title: Splunk
item.description:
Splunk made machine data searchable. It ingests logs, metrics, and events from servers, applications, networks, and cloud services, indexes them, and lets users search and visualize with its Search Processing Language. Companies use it to troubleshoot outages, monitor performance, and investigate security incidents, and it has been a mainstay of security operations centers for many years.

The product line includes Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud for core analytics, Enterprise Security as a SIEM for threat detection, and observability tools for infrastructure and application monitoring. AI features include an assistant that helps write searches from plain language and summarizes findings, and machine learning for anomaly detection. Cisco acquired Splunk and is integrating it with its networking and security products.

item.title: Stripe Agentic Commerce Suite
item.description:
As AI agents begin to shop and pay on behalf of people, merchants and payment systems need a way to handle it. Stripe’s suite helps businesses become discoverable to agents: a merchant uploads a product catalog, chooses which agent platforms to sell through, and Stripe handles discovery, checkout, and payments.

It builds on open protocols. The Agentic Commerce Protocol, developed with OpenAI, defines how an agent and a merchant negotiate a checkout. The Machine Payments Protocol, written with Tempo, lets agents and services coordinate payments in code, including small recurring transactions. Stripe also supports an agent wallet and stablecoin payments over the x402 protocol, and it issues limited-use tokens so an agent can spend within set limits.

item.title: Teachable
item.description:
Teachable is a platform for people who want to sell what they know. A creator uploads video lessons, text, and quizzes, organizes them into a course, sets a price, and publishes it on a branded school site. Students enroll, pay, and track their progress, and the creator gets sales and engagement data.

The platform handles the business side. It processes payments in many currencies, supports subscriptions, bundles, and coupons, and offers tools for affiliate programs and email marketing. Coaching products and downloadable files can be sold alongside courses, and certificates reward completion. AI features help draft course outlines and descriptions.

item.title: Thinkific
item.description:
Thinkific is an online course platform. Creators build courses from video, audio, text, and quizzes, organize them into chapters, and host them on a site with their own branding and domain. Students log in to learn, and the platform tracks completion and issues certificates.

Features extend beyond courses. Memberships and communities keep learners engaged, bundles and subscriptions provide pricing options, and integrations connect with email tools, payment processors, and Zapier. Businesses also use Thinkific to train customers, partners, and employees, and AI tools help generate course outlines and quiz questions.

item.title: Twilio ConversationRelay
item.description:
ConversationRelay connects phone calls to AI. When a call arrives on a Twilio number, the service converts the caller’s speech to text in real time and streams it over a WebSocket to the developer’s server. The server sends text back, which Twilio converts into speech, so the caller hears a natural response. This lets teams plug in any large language model and their own business logic.

Twilio manages the hard parts of voice. It handles interruptions when a caller speaks over the agent, supports multiple languages and voice providers, and can transfer the call to a human with the transcript. It also offers a no-code Studio widget for simpler flows, plus compliance support for regulated industries, including options for HIPAA and PCI. A reporting feature gives insight into latency and where agents struggle.

item.title: Zapier MCP
item.description:
Zapier MCP turns Zapier’s app library into tools an AI can use. You create an MCP server, choose the apps and actions you want to allow, such as sending a Slack message, adding a row in Google Sheets, or creating a CRM contact, and connect that server to a compatible client. The assistant can then call those actions during a conversation.

This avoids writing custom integrations. Zapier already handles authentication and the quirks of each app’s API, so connecting an assistant to a new service is a matter of adding an action and authorizing your account. You control the scope, and each call uses your connected account, which helps limit what the AI can touch.

item.title: Jobber
item.description:
Jobber is built for small service companies such as lawn care, cleaning, plumbing, and locksmith businesses. Owners send quotes, schedule jobs on a calendar, dispatch crews, and invoice customers, with a mobile app for the crew to see their route, take notes, and collect payment on site.

Client-facing features help win and keep work. Customers can request services online, approve quotes, pay invoices, and receive reminders and arrival notices, and a client hub keeps their history together. Automations send follow-ups and review requests. An AI assistant drafts messages and helps convert rough notes into a clear quote.

item.title: Kajabi
item.description:
Kajabi is an all-in-one platform for knowledge businesses. A creator builds a site, sells courses, memberships, coaching, and digital downloads, collects payments, runs email campaigns, and hosts a community, all from one dashboard instead of stitching together several tools.

Marketing and automation are built in. Landing pages, funnels, email sequences, and a pipeline for leads let creators sell without extra software. The AI assistant helps write copy, plan courses, and generate emails, and analytics show revenue and engagement. Mobile apps for members are available.

item.title: Moveworks
item.description:
Moveworks brings an assistant to employee support. Workers ask for help in Slack, Teams, or a portal, and the system understands the request, finds the answer in company knowledge, or completes the action by connecting to IT and HR systems. Common examples are unlocking an account, requesting software, or finding a policy.

The company grew by focusing on large enterprises and on language understanding specific to workplace requests. It added generative AI and agent capabilities, with a platform for building custom agents and connecting to many business systems.

item.title: Nemotron 3 Diarization
item.description: NVIDIA released Nemotron 3 Diarization on September 23, 2026, a 100-million-parameter open-weight model that tracks up to eight overlapping speakers in real-time streaming audio. It targets call-center and meeting-transcription pipelines that need to know who said what as the audio comes in, rather than after the fact.

item.title: Noterro
item.description:
Noterro is built for small bodywork and rehab practices. Clients book online and fill in intake forms before arriving, and therapists record sessions with notes. An AI feature turns a few prompts into a structured SOAP note, saving time at the end of each appointment.

Other tools cover everyday needs: scheduling, reminders, payments, packages and memberships, and insurance claims where relevant. Reports track revenue and client retention.

Noterro is paid, with plans per practitioner. It is aimed at solo practitioners and small clinics. Alternatives include Jane, Cliniko, MassageBook, Vagaro, and SimplePractice. Noterro suits manual therapists who want simpler admin.

item.title: SimplePractice
item.description:
SimplePractice is widely used by solo and small group private practices. Clients book appointments online, complete intake forms in a portal, and join video sessions, while clinicians keep notes, treatment plans, and billing in the same system. Insurance claims can be submitted electronically.

AI features help clinicians write progress notes from session details and speed up documentation, which is a chief burden for therapists. The platform offers reminders, reporting, and a client app for messaging and payments.

item.title: StyleSeat
item.description:
StyleSeat serves independent beauty professionals. Clients search for stylists, browse portfolios and reviews, and book appointments, while professionals manage their calendar, take deposits, and process payments through the platform.

The marketplace helps new clients find providers, and the business tools handle reminders, no-show protection, and client records. Recommendations use location and preference data to match clients.

StyleSeat has a subscription for professionals and fees on some transactions. Fees for marketplace clients can be a concern for stylists with an existing following. Alternatives include Vagaro, Fresha, Booksy, Square Appointments, and Glossgenius. StyleSeat suits independent stylists and barbers.

item.title: Vagaro
item.description:
Vagaro runs the front desk for beauty and wellness businesses. Clients book online or through a marketplace app, staff manage calendars, take payments, and track inventory. Reminders and no-show protection reduce lost appointments.

Marketing tools include email and text campaigns, loyalty programs, and a presence on the Vagaro marketplace. AI answers calls and messages, helps book appointments, and suggests promotions.

Vagaro charges a monthly fee per business, with add-ons and payment processing fees. Alternatives include Fresha, Booksy, StyleSeat, Square Appointments, and Mindbody. Vagaro suits salons, spas, and studios.

item.title: OpenAI Presence
item.description:
Presence aims to let companies put OpenAI-powered agents on the front line of conversations. Businesses configure agents that talk with customers by phone or chat and handle employee requests, connecting them to company systems so they can look up information and take actions.

The platform combines the models with enterprise features: tools for building and testing agents, integrations, monitoring, and controls to keep agents within policy. It competes with specialized customer service AI vendors and with platforms from other model providers.

item.title: Amazon Nova 2 Pro
item.description: Amazon Nova 2 Pro is the first refresh of the Nova Pro tier since the original family launched at re:Invent 2024, and it’s exclusive to AWS Bedrock like the rest of the line. It moves the context window up to 500,000 tokens and adds video understanding alongside text and image, priced at $1.50 per million input tokens and $6.00 per million output tokens, a jump from the original Nova Pro that reflects the added capability.

item.title: Command A2
item.description:
Command A2 succeeds Command A as Cohere’s flagship model, keeping the same enterprise-first pitch: strong retrieval-augmented generation, tool use, and multilingual support over chasing chatbot benchmarks. It’s priced at $2.50 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, and it’s reachable through Cohere’s own API as well as AWS Bedrock, Azure AI Foundry, and Oracle Cloud, the same multi-cloud distribution Cohere has relied on since Command R.

Cohere continues to sell mainly to enterprises building internal search and document-QA systems rather than consumer-facing products, and Command A2’s improvements are aimed squarely at that audience: better grounding on retrieved documents and more reliable citation of sources, both areas where the company has staked its reputation against larger labs with flashier general-purpose models.

item.title: Baidu Qianfan
item.description:
Qianfan is Baidu’s cloud platform for building with large models. Companies can call Baidu’s ERNIE models and a selection of third-party and open models through a common API, then build applications such as chatbots, search over internal documents, and automated workflows. The platform covers the steps in between, including prompt engineering, fine-tuning, evaluation, and deployment.

It includes tools for agents and retrieval, with knowledge-base features that let applications answer from a company’s own data, plus plugins and workflows for connecting to business systems. Qianfan is used heavily within China, where Baidu offers local hosting and compliance with domestic regulations.

item.title: Cohere North
item.description:
North is Cohere’s platform for putting agents to work inside companies. Employees use a chat interface and can build agents without code for tasks in HR, finance, IT, and other areas, connecting them to the apps and documents they already use. Search across company data is powered by Cohere’s own retrieval technology.

Security and control are the main pitch. Organizations can deploy North in a private cloud, on premises, or in air-gapped settings, which appeals to banks, governments, and defense contractors with strict data rules. Cohere designs the models for enterprise use and works with customers on custom solutions.

item.title: Dataiku
item.description:
Dataiku aims to let analysts, data scientists, and engineers work in the same environment. Teams connect to data sources, clean and prepare data with visual recipes or code, build models, and deploy them as applications or services. The visual interface lowers the barrier for business users, while coders can use notebooks and libraries.

The platform has added tools for generative AI, including connecting to language models, building retrieval applications, and creating agents. Governance features track models and projects, assess risk, and document decisions, which large organizations need to meet internal and regulatory requirements.

item.title: Palantir AIP
item.description:
AIP, the Artificial Intelligence Platform, is Palantir’s layer for putting language models to work on an organization’s data. It builds on Palantir’s ontology, a structured model of a company’s objects, such as orders, machines, and customers, and the actions that can be taken on them. Models can then read and act within that governed model instead of working on raw text.

Customers build agents and applications that automate tasks, answer questions, and support decisions in areas like supply chain, healthcare, defense, and manufacturing. Controls around access, logging, and human approval aim to make AI usable in sensitive settings. Palantir runs engagement programs that help customers reach production quickly.

item.title: Tencent Cloud ADP
item.description:
Tencent Cloud ADP gives companies tools to create agents. Users connect knowledge bases for retrieval, design workflows with a visual editor, and combine agents that work together. Models include Tencent’s Hunyuan family and others.

Typical applications are customer service, internal assistants, and process automation. The platform includes tools for testing and monitoring and integrates with Tencent’s ecosystem, including WeChat and enterprise messaging.

It is sold on usage-based pricing within Tencent Cloud. Outside China, availability and support are more limited, and organizations must consider data residency. Alternatives include Alibaba Cloud’s Bailian, Baidu Qianfan, ByteDance’s Volcano Engine, Dify, and AWS Bedrock Agents. Tencent Cloud ADP suits companies building agents on Tencent Cloud.

item.title: Amazon Nova Pro
item.description: Amazon Nova Pro is the flagship general-purpose model in Amazon’s Nova family, announced in December 2024 and served through Amazon Bedrock. It takes text, image, and video input, returns text, and supports a 300,000-token context window, priced at $0.80 per million input tokens and $3.20 per million output tokens. Amazon positioned it as the model for complex tasks such as multi-step reasoning, document analysis, and agentic workflows where Nova Lite’s lighter capability isn’t enough.

item.title: Arctic
item.description: Arctic is a large language model that Snowflake released in April 2024, built for enterprise work like SQL generation, coding, and instruction following rather than general chat. It uses a mixture-of-experts design with 480 billion total parameters spread across 128 experts, but only about 17 billion are active for any given token, which keeps inference costs down relative to dense models of similar scale. Snowflake released both the base and instruct checkpoints under an Apache 2.0 license, so the weights can be self-hosted or run through Snowflake Cortex. On the Spider text-to-SQL benchmark it scored around 79% accuracy, and Snowflake pitched it as a way to bring capable open models into data warehouses without sending queries to a third-party API. It trades off a shorter 4K context window and weaker general chat ability against strong performance on the narrow enterprise tasks it was built for.

item.title: Born to Found
item.description:
Born to Found guides first-time founders through the early journey. It divides company building into stages, such as validating an idea, building a first product, and finding customers, and supplies playbooks and checklists for each, so a founder knows what to focus on at their point.

An AI coach answers questions and reviews work, drawing on the founder’s stage and project details. This offers a low-cost alternative to mentors for people who lack access to experienced advisors, and a structure to keep going when the path is unclear.

item.title: Command A
item.description: Command A is Cohere’s flagship large language model, released in March 2025 at the top of its Command lineup. It has 111 billion parameters and a 256,000 token context window, and Cohere built it to run on as few as two GPUs while matching or beating larger competing models on agentic, multilingual, and coding tasks. It scores 85.5 on MMLU, putting it in the same range as GPT-4o and Llama 3.3 70B. Command A is tuned for retrieval-augmented generation and tool use, and it’s available through the Cohere platform and Azure AI at $2.50 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, or as a self-hosted deployment for enterprises that need to keep data on their own infrastructure. Cohere later added Command A+, a larger 218 billion parameter model, to the same family.

item.title: Command Light
item.description: Command Light is Cohere’s smallest and fastest model from the original Command family, released alongside Embed v3 in November 2023. It has around 6 billion parameters and a 4,096 token context window, and Cohere designed it for applications that need low latency and lower cost rather than top-tier reasoning. It was priced at $0.30 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens through the Cohere API. Cohere deprecated Command Light in September 2025 along with several other early Command models, and now points users toward Command R, Command R+, or Command A, calling Command A the strongest performer across the board. It remains documented here as a legacy option that some existing integrations may still reference.

item.title: Command R+
item.description: Command R+ is Cohere’s flagship large language model, built for enterprise use cases centered on retrieval-augmented generation, tool use, and multi-step agent workflows. It launched in April 2024 with 104 billion parameters and a 128,000-token context window, then received a refreshed version in August 2024 that cut latency and raised throughput on the same hardware footprint. The model supports 10 languages for business use and ships with citation generation built in, so answers grounded in retrieved documents come with source references attached. Cohere positions it against GPT-4-class models for RAG-heavy deployments rather than as a general chatbot, and it is available both through Cohere’s own API and as open weights on Hugging Face under a non-commercial license.

item.title: Firefly Image 3
item.description: Firefly Image 3 is Adobe’s image generation model, introduced in April 2024 as an upgrade over the original Firefly model that launched in 2023. Adobe trained it to be commercially safe, meaning it draws only on licensed Adobe Stock content, public domain material, and other content Adobe has rights to use, which lets business customers generate images without the copyright uncertainty tied to models trained on scraped web data. It improved on its predecessor with better prompt understanding, sharper detail, and Structure Reference and Style Reference tools that let users guide output using an existing image’s composition or visual style. Adobe built it into Photoshop, Illustrator, Adobe Express, and the standalone Firefly web app, with API access for enterprise integrations. Adobe has continued to ship newer Firefly image models since, and it retired Image 3 from its model picker in 2026 in favor of those successors.

item.title: Firefly Video
item.description: Firefly Video is Adobe’s text-to-video and image-to-video model, announced at Adobe MAX in October 2024 and opened to public beta through the standalone Firefly web app in February 2025. Adobe positions it as the first widely available video model built to be commercially safe, trained on licensed and public domain sources so businesses can use its output without copyright exposure. Inside Premiere Pro, it powers Generative Extend, a feature editors use to stretch a clip to cover a gap in footage, smooth a jump cut, or hold a shot longer without reshooting. Through 2025, Adobe added camera motion controls, start-frame image uploads, and prompt-based editing of existing footage, moving the tool from pure generation toward directed video editing. It remains in beta as of mid-2026, with Adobe rolling out updates alongside its other Firefly models rather than shipping a single finished version.

item.title: Granite 13B
item.description: Granite 13B is one of IBM’s first foundation models built for its watsonx enterprise AI platform, announced on September 7, 2023 alongside a family of Granite models aimed at business use cases rather than general chat. It has 13 billion parameters, uses multi-query attention with learned position embeddings, and was trained with the tokenizer from EleutherAI’s GPT-NeoX-20B, giving it an 8,192 token context window. IBM built it for tasks like document summarization, question answering, and text classification inside regulated industries such as banking and insurance, and it came with IBM’s standard indemnification for customers worried about training-data copyright exposure, a selling point competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic did not offer at the time. Granite 13B was proprietary and accessible only through watsonx, distinguishing it from IBM’s later Granite 3 generation, which shifted toward openly licensed weights on Hugging Face. It has since been superseded by newer Granite versions as IBM’s enterprise AI lineup moved toward open weights and broader benchmark parity with mainstream models.

item.title: Granite 3.0
item.description: Granite 3.0 is IBM’s third-generation family of open language models, released on October 21, 2024 for enterprise use cases like customer service, cybersecurity, and RAG pipelines. The lineup includes dense 2B and 8B models trained on 12 trillion tokens plus 1B and 3B mixture-of-experts variants, all released under the Apache 2.0 license so they can be fine-tuned and deployed commercially without restriction. IBM positioned Granite 3.0 against similarly sized models from Meta and Mistral, reporting competitive or better scores on benchmarks covering reasoning, code, and math while keeping the models small enough to run cheaply on standard GPUs. The initial release shipped with a 4K context window, later extended to 128K tokens in the Granite 3.1 update released in December 2024. Granite 3.0 is available through Hugging Face, Ollama, and IBM’s watsonx platform, and it forms the base for IBM’s related Granite Guardian, Code, and Vision models.

item.title: Granite Embedding
item.description: Granite Embedding is IBM’s family of text embedding models for retrieval and semantic search, built to plug into enterprise RAG systems on watsonx or self-hosted infrastructure. The 278M-parameter multilingual variant covers twelve languages including English, German, Japanese, Arabic, and Chinese, and it produces 768-dimension vectors from inputs up to 512 tokens. IBM trained it with contrastive fine-tuning, knowledge distillation, and model merging over a mix of open relevance-pair datasets and IBM’s own curated data, favoring sources with permissive, enterprise-friendly licensing. Like the rest of the Granite line, the embedding models ship under Apache 2.0 and are distributed through Hugging Face, Ollama, and IBM watsonx, competing with other open embedding families like BGE and GTE on retrieval benchmarks while emphasizing compliance and traceable training data for regulated customers.

item.title: Granite Guardian
item.description: Granite Guardian is IBM’s family of safety models, built to sit alongside a primary LLM and flag risky prompts or responses before they reach a user or an application. It launched with Granite 3.0 in October 2024 in 2B and 8B sizes, both fine-tuned from the base Granite instruct models rather than trained from scratch, and it checks for harms cataloged in IBM’s AI Risk Atlas: things like jailbreak attempts, profanity, social bias, violence, and hallucinated tool calls or retrieval results in agentic workflows. IBM also ships a much smaller 38M-parameter HAP (hate, abuse, profanity) variant for teams that need guardrailing under tighter latency or cost budgets. Granite Guardian is open-weighted under Apache 2.0 and distributed through Hugging Face, Ollama, NVIDIA, and watsonx, and later updates, including a 3.3 release and a 4.1 release with support for user-defined judging criteria, extended the same approach to newer Granite base models.

item.title: Granite Vision
item.description: Granite Vision is IBM’s compact vision-language model, released as part of the Granite 3.2 update in February 2025 and built specifically for visual document understanding rather than general image chat. At 2 billion parameters, it reads tables, charts, infographics, plots, and scanned documents and turns them into structured text, targeting benchmarks like DocVQA and ChartQA where IBM says it matches open models several times its size. The small footprint is deliberate: IBM designed it for everyday enterprise workloads, such as parsing invoices or extracting data from reports, where running a large multimodal model isn’t practical or affordable. It supports a 16K token context window, is open-weighted under Apache 2.0, and is distributed through Hugging Face and IBM watsonx, with later versions (3.3 and the Granite 4.0 vision variants) building on the same document-focused design.

item.title: Luminous
item.description: Luminous is a family of large language models from the German company Aleph Alpha, first released in April 2022 in three sizes: Luminous Base, Extended, and Supreme, with the largest Supreme tier reaching 70 billion parameters by that August. Aleph Alpha built Luminous as a multilingual model with an early focus on European languages and enterprise use cases where regulatory compliance and data residency in the EU matter. Its most distinctive feature is explainability: Luminous can point back to the specific passages in its input that a given output was based on, a source-attribution capability aimed at industries like law, finance, and government that need to audit AI-generated answers. Aleph Alpha positions Luminous as a European alternative to US-based models from OpenAI and Google, sold mainly to enterprise and public-sector customers through its own API rather than to general consumers.

item.title: AICode
item.description:
AICode targets a problem many AI coding tools handle poorly: older systems with hundreds of files and years of accumulated decisions. Where an assistant that autocompletes in a single file struggles, a tool built for legacy code needs to understand how modules depend on each other and what a change will affect.

The pitch includes helping developers navigate unfamiliar code, explain what a function does and why, plan refactors, and write documentation or tests. Teams that inherit a system with little documentation can use that kind of help to get productive faster. Work on large code usually depends on good context retrieval and on careful human review of suggested changes.

item.title: C3.ai
item.description:
C3.ai builds packaged AI applications and a platform for developing them. Instead of starting from scratch, a company can adopt an application for a defined problem, such as predicting when equipment will fail, detecting fraud, or optimizing inventory, and connect it to their data. The platform provides tools for data integration, modeling, and deployment.

The company has moved to add generative AI. Its offerings include tools that let users ask questions about enterprise data in natural language and agent features for business workflows. Customers include utilities, manufacturers, banks, and defense and government agencies, where large-scale deployments are common.

item.title: SambaNova
item.description:
SambaNova designs custom chips, called reconfigurable dataflow units, along with the software and systems around them. The goal is high-speed inference and training for large language models at lower power than general-purpose GPU setups.

Its cloud service offers fast access to open models through an API, and enterprises can deploy systems on premises for data control. Government and large organizations are among its customers.

SambaNova is sold on usage-based cloud pricing and system contracts. The company has faced a competitive field of chip makers and has been the subject of reports about funding and acquisition talks, so check its status. Alternatives include Groq, Cerebras, NVIDIA, Together AI, and Fireworks AI. SambaNova suits organizations needing fast inference.

item.title: Seismic
item.description:
Seismic organizes marketing and sales content so reps can find and use it. Instead of searching shared drives, a seller gets recommended decks, case studies, and playbooks based on the deal stage and customer, and can assemble personalized presentations quickly.

Analytics show which content gets used and which correlates with wins, and engagement data tells sellers how buyers interact with shared materials. Coaching and training modules, and AI that writes tailored messages and summaries, add to the suite.

item.title: Sprinklr
item.description:
Sprinklr serves very large organizations. It manages publishing across social channels, listens for brand mentions, handles customer care across messaging and voice, and analyzes market trends, using a shared data layer so teams see the whole customer picture.

AI runs through the platform: models classify conversations, detect sentiment, route cases, suggest replies, and generate content, and agents handle some customer interactions. Governance tools suit regulated industries and large teams.

Sprinklr is sold on enterprise subscriptions, with high cost and complexity. Alternatives include Hootsuite, Sprout Social, Khoros, Emplifi, and Salesforce. Sprinklr suits large brands managing many channels.

item.title: Stack AI
item.description:
Stack AI offers a visual builder for AI workflows. Users drag together components such as inputs, language models, document search, and outputs, then connect them to enterprise tools. The result can be deployed as a chatbot, form, or API.

Common cases include document processing, internal knowledge assistants, and support triage. The platform emphasizes security and governance, with options for private deployment. Templates give a starting point.

Stack AI has a free tier and paid plans. Workflows need testing and monitoring. Alternatives include Relevance AI, Dify, Flowise, n8n, and Microsoft Copilot Studio. Stack AI suits business teams building AI workflows without code.

item.title: SYSTRAN
item.description:
SYSTRAN is among the oldest names in machine translation. Its modern products use neural models, offered as an API, a desktop app, and server software that can run inside an organization’s own network. This matters for sensitive documents.

Customization lets organizations tune translation to their terminology, and the platform handles many file formats and language pairs. Government and corporate customers use it for large volumes of content.

SYSTRAN is sold by subscription and license. General-purpose language models now compete in translation quality. Alternatives include DeepL, Google Cloud Translation, Microsoft Translator, Amazon Translate, and Lilt. SYSTRAN suits organizations needing private, deployable translation.

item.title: Writer
item.description:
Writer targets large organizations that need AI output to stay on brand and compliant. Teams set style guides, terminology, and rules, and the system applies them as people draft, with checks for claims and tone. A knowledge graph lets AI answer from company data.

The company builds its own Palmyra language models and a platform for building agents that handle multi-step work across tools. Governance features such as permissions, logging, and fact checks support regulated industries.

item.title: Yellow.ai
item.description:
Yellow.ai builds AI agents for customer and employee service. A company connects it to systems such as CRMs and ticketing, trains it on content, and deploys across websites, messaging apps, and phone lines. The agents answer questions and complete tasks in many languages.

The platform emphasizes multilingual support, strong in markets such as India, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Tools for building, testing, and monitoring agents, along with analytics, support operations teams. Handoff to human agents is built in.

item.title: Bonsai
item.description:
Bonsai bundles the paperwork of independent work. A freelancer sends a proposal, converts it into a contract with e-signature, tracks time or milestones, sends an invoice, and receives payment. A client portal keeps everything in one place, which helps a one-person business look established.

Additional tools cover running the business. Expense tracking, tax estimates, and banking features support finances, and workflow automations send reminders for unpaid invoices. AI helps draft contract language and project descriptions. Templates are available for design, consulting, development, and other fields.

item.title: ServiceTitan
item.description:
ServiceTitan is built for home service trades. Call center staff book jobs, dispatchers assign technicians, technicians use a mobile app to quote and invoice with good-better-best pricing, and the office tracks job costs, marketing, and payroll. Everything ties to one customer record.

Data and AI help companies grow. Tools score inbound calls, flag missed opportunities, recommend pricing, and predict technician performance, and agents assist with booking and follow-ups. Reporting shows revenue per technician and marketing return.

item.title: Agiloft
item.description:
Agiloft is a configurable system for managing contracts from request to renewal. Teams create agreements from templates and clause libraries, route them through approvals, negotiate with redlining, collect signatures, and store them in a searchable repository. Alerts remind owners of renewals and obligations, and reports show how contracts are performing, so legal, procurement, and sales teams share a single source of truth.

Its design emphasizes flexibility without custom coding. Organizations can adjust fields, workflows, and rules through no-code tools, which suits companies with unusual processes, and it connects with systems such as Salesforce, SAP, and DocuSign. AI features extract data from existing contracts, identify risky or missing clauses, summarize agreements, and let users ask questions in plain language, which speeds up migration from messy archives.

item.title: Amwell
item.description:
Amwell provides the technology behind a lot of virtual care. Hospitals and health systems use it to run telehealth programs for their own patients, health plans offer it as a benefit, and employers use it to give workers access to remote visits. Patients can see a clinician by video for urgent care, primary care, behavioral health, and specialty care, with scheduling, intake, and visit tools in one platform.

It also offers services around the visit. These include a hospital-grade platform for remote consultations within hospitals, digital programs for chronic conditions, and a network of clinicians for companies that don’t have their own. AI features help with intake, triage, and documentation, and the platform integrates with electronic health records. Its ability to be customized for each client is a selling point.

item.title: Appen
item.description:
Appen is one of the long-standing companies behind AI training data. Machine learning models need large amounts of labeled examples, such as transcribed speech, tagged images, ranked answers, and annotated documents, and Appen supplies them through a global crowd of contributors plus managed teams. Its customers have included major technology companies, and its work has fed search, voice assistants, and recommendation systems.

The services now lean toward generative AI. Appen provides data for aligning large language models, such as human preference rankings, expert-written examples, and red-teaming to find unsafe behavior. It also offers multimodal and speech datasets, coding data, and model evaluation services that test how a system performs in many languages and regions. A platform manages the workflows, quality checks, and contributor payments.

item.title: ArcGIS
item.description: ArcGIS is the leading commercial GIS platform. Governments, utilities, environmental agencies, city planners, and businesses use it to collect location data, display it on maps, and analyze spatial relationships, such as which neighborhoods lie within a flood zone or where to place a new store. The product family includes ArcGIS Pro for desktop analysis, ArcGIS Online as a cloud service for building and sharing maps, and ArcGIS Enterprise for organizations that run their own servers.

item.title: BetterUp
item.description:
BetterUp sells coaching to organizations as a benefit for employees. Each person is matched with a coach based on goals such as becoming a better manager, handling stress, improving communication, or preparing for a promotion. Sessions take place by video, with coaches who are credentialed and trained in a consistent method. The company also includes assessments, programs for managers, and group sessions, and it publishes research on its results.

Technology plays a growing role. AI tools supplement human coaches by offering reflection prompts, summarizing sessions, suggesting next steps, and giving employees an always-available assistant for quick questions. Dashboards give employers aggregate data on participation and outcomes, without exposing individual conversations. Programs can be scaled for small teams or an entire company.

item.title: Deepdub
item.description: Deepdub works with studios, streamers, and media companies that need content in many languages. Its technology translates the dialogue and generates new speech in the target language, in a voice that matches the original performer, with timing that fits the picture. The goal is dubbing that carries over emotion and character, not the flat voice of a basic text-to-speech engine. It supports over a hundred languages and uses licensed voices, which matters for rights and union considerations.

item.title: Doxy.me
item.description:
Doxy.me gives clinicians a simple way to see patients by video. A provider gets a personal link; patients click it, enter a virtual waiting room, and join the visit in their browser with no account or app installation. That simplicity matters for patients who are not comfortable with technology, and it suits therapists, physicians, dietitians, speech and physical therapists, and other practitioners.

Beyond video, the paid tiers add features that clinics need. These include a customizable waiting room, patient check-in, screen sharing, group sessions, text message reminders, payments, and integrations with electronic health record systems. Administrators can manage a team of providers under one account, and the platform includes business associate agreements that healthcare organizations need under HIPAA. Newer AI tools offer note-taking from visits.

item.title: Geotab
item.description:
Geotab makes the small devices that plug into vehicles and report what they do. A device in the diagnostic port records location, speed, harsh braking, idling, engine fault codes, and more, and sends the data to the cloud, where fleet managers view it on maps and dashboards. Companies with delivery vans, service trucks, buses, and long-haul trucks use it to track vehicles, optimize routes, and reduce costs.

Analytics turn the data into insights. Driver scoring identifies risky behavior and supports coaching, maintenance alerts flag vehicles that need service based on engine data, and fuel and emissions reports support efficiency and electric vehicle planning. AI features include an assistant that answers questions about fleet data in natural language, and models that predict problems and rank safety risks. A marketplace of third-party apps extends the platform, and compliance tools support electronic logging rules.

item.title: Lexalytics
item.description: Lexalytics builds natural language processing for businesses that need to make sense of large amounts of text. Its Salience engine reads reviews, survey comments, support tickets, social posts, and call transcripts and returns structured information: whether the sentiment is positive or negative, which products or people are mentioned, what themes recur, and what the author intends. Analysts can then count, trend, and compare these signals instead of reading comments one by one.

item.title: Mapbox
item.description:
Mapbox is the mapping toolkit behind many apps. Developers use its SDKs to embed interactive maps in websites and in iOS and Android apps, with control over styles, layers, and data. Mapbox Studio lets designers customize map appearance, while vector tiles keep maps fast and sharp. Companies in logistics, travel, real estate, and mobility use it to show routes, locations, and live data.

The platform goes beyond display. APIs handle geocoding and search, turn-by-turn navigation, route optimization, isochrones that show how far you can get in a given time, and traffic-aware directions. A navigation SDK supports in-app guidance, and tools for working with large geospatial datasets allow analysis and visualization. Machine learning is used for features such as map matching and road data updates, and recent products add AI assistants for developers.

item.title: Okta
item.description:
Okta is one of the best-known providers of cloud identity. Companies use it as the central place where employees sign in to their applications: one login gives access to hundreds of apps through single sign-on, and multi-factor authentication adds protection against stolen passwords. The Universal Directory stores identities and groups, and lifecycle management automates giving people the right access when they join, change roles, or leave.

The platform covers more of the identity problem over time. Adaptive policies check device and context before allowing access, governance tools handle access reviews and requests, and privileged access tools protect administrator accounts. Okta also owns Auth0 for customer-facing apps. As companies deploy AI agents that act on behalf of users, Okta has added features for giving these agents their own identities and managing what they may do.

item.title: OneTrust
item.description:
OneTrust helps large organizations manage the rules about data. Its best-known product handles consent: the cookie banners and preference centers that appear on websites and apps and record what visitors agree to. Privacy teams use other modules to respond to data subject requests such as access and deletion, map where personal data is stored, run privacy impact assessments, and show regulators that they follow laws like GDPR and CCPA.

The platform has expanded into broader governance, risk, and compliance. Tools cover third-party and vendor risk, security and IT risk, ethics and policy management, and environmental and social reporting. A growing area is AI governance: inventorying the AI systems an organization uses, assessing their risks, and tracking compliance with emerging rules such as the EU AI Act. AI features in the platform help classify data and automate assessments.

item.title: Stripe
item.description: Stripe began as a way for developers to accept card payments with a few lines of code and has become the payment layer for much of the internet. Businesses use it to take cards and local payment methods online and in person, bill customers on subscription plans, send invoices, and pay out sellers on marketplaces. Its documentation and libraries are widely admired, which is why startups tend to adopt it first. It operates in many countries and currencies.

item.title: AI21 Labs
item.description: AI21 Labs was founded by AI researchers in Tel Aviv and has been building language models since before ChatGPT made them mainstream. Its best-known models are the Jamba family, which blend a state-space architecture called Mamba with transformer layers. The aim is a model that handles very long documents with less memory and faster output than a standard transformer of similar size. Several Jamba versions have been released with open weights.

item.title: Amazon Bedrock
item.description: Bedrock is how many companies on AWS use large language models without running any model infrastructure. Instead of signing separate contracts with each AI lab, you pick from a catalog of models from providers such as Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, and Amazon itself, and call them through one API. The data stays inside your AWS account, which matters to teams with security, privacy, and compliance requirements, and it works with the IAM, networking, and logging tools they already use.

item.title: AppSheet
item.description:
AppSheet lets people create business apps without programming. You point it at data in Google Sheets, Excel, a database, or another source, and AppSheet generates an app with views, forms, and actions. Typical uses include field service, inspections, inventory tracking, approvals, and data collection, where workers need to capture information on a phone, with photos, barcodes, GPS, and signatures.

AI helps create apps. Gemini can build an app from a plain-language description, and an assistant can suggest improvements and write expressions. Automation features, called bots, trigger actions such as sending emails, updating records, or creating documents when data changes, and integrations connect with Google Workspace, Apps Script, and other services. Governance features cover access control and deployment for organizations.

item.title: AutoGen
item.description:
AutoGen made multi-agent applications approachable. Developers define agents with roles, such as a coder, a reviewer, and a user proxy, and let them converse to solve a problem. Agents can write and run code, call tools, and ask humans for input, and the framework manages the message passing between them.

The project began at Microsoft Research and attracted a large community. A visual tool, AutoGen Studio, let people prototype agent teams without code. Over time, Microsoft consolidated its efforts, pointing new projects to the Microsoft Agent Framework, which combines ideas from AutoGen and Semantic Kernel, and describing AutoGen as being in maintenance mode.

item.title: Azure OpenAI Service
item.description:
Azure OpenAI is OpenAI’s model lineup delivered through Microsoft’s cloud. Companies use it to get the same families of language, reasoning, image, and audio models, but under Azure’s terms, billing, and security controls. For regulated industries and large enterprises, that matters: the data is processed inside Azure, can be isolated on a private network, and is covered by Microsoft’s compliance certifications and service-level agreement.

Development happens in Microsoft Foundry, where you deploy a model, test it in a playground, and connect it to your own data and tools. Available features include fine-tuning, content filtering, tool and function calling, retrieval over company documents, and tracing. Deployments come in several types, such as standard pay-as-you-go, batch, and provisioned throughput, which reserves capacity for steady workloads with predictable latency. Foundry also offers non-OpenAI models, so teams can compare options in one place.

item.title: Betterworks
item.description:
Betterworks supports how companies manage performance throughout the year. Employees set goals or OKRs that link to company priorities, managers hold regular check-ins, and feedback and recognition are captured along the way. Review cycles then draw on this record, so evaluations rely less on recent memory.

AI features help with the writing and analysis. An assistant can improve goal statements, summarize a year of feedback into review drafts, and suggest coaching points, while analytics show goal progress and engagement across teams. Integrations connect with HR systems like Workday and collaboration tools such as Slack and Microsoft Teams.

item.title: BigCommerce
item.description:
BigCommerce provides the pieces needed to sell online. A merchant sets up a storefront with themes, manages products and inventory, accepts payments, calculates shipping and tax, and sells across channels such as Amazon, eBay, Google, social platforms, and marketplaces. Many features that other platforms handle through apps, such as product variants, reviews, and discounts, are built in, which keeps costs more predictable.

It stands out in two areas. It supports B2B commerce with features like customer-specific pricing, quotes, and bulk ordering, and it’s designed for headless setups in which the storefront is built separately and connected through APIs, which suits brands wanting a custom front end. AI tools help generate product descriptions, support merchandising, and optimize search, and an ecosystem of apps and partners extends the platform.

item.title: Brandwatch
item.description:
Brandwatch is used by marketing, communications, and research teams to understand what people say online. It collects posts and mentions from social networks, news sites, forums, blogs, and reviews, and lets analysts build searches to track a brand, a competitor, a campaign, or a topic. Dashboards show volume over time, sentiment, demographics, top influencers, and emerging themes, which helps with campaign measurement, crisis monitoring, and product feedback.

AI plays a role in making sense of the data. Language models classify sentiment and topics, group conversations into themes, summarize large sets of posts, and answer questions about the findings in natural language. Image recognition finds logos in pictures posted without any text. Alerts warn teams when mentions spike, and the social management side supports publishing and responding to messages from one place.

item.title: Cerebras
item.description:
Cerebras took an unusual approach to AI hardware. Instead of cutting a silicon wafer into many small chips, it builds a single enormous chip from the whole wafer, which holds an enormous amount of compute and on-chip memory. That design reduces the data movement between chips that slows down large models, and lets it generate tokens at very high speeds.

The company sells its systems and operates a cloud inference service where developers call open models through an API, with fast responses that suit agents, coding tools, and real-time applications. It has partnerships with AI labs and cloud providers, and supports training as well as inference. Developers can try the API with a free tier and then pay by usage, often at competitive per-token rates.

item.title: Clari
item.description:
Clari began as a tool to make sales forecasting more reliable. It reads CRM data and signals from email, calendar, and calls to show how deals are progressing, then rolls those into a forecast that managers can inspect by team, region, and stage. The goal is to replace spreadsheet-based forecast calls with data that people trust.

AI helps spot trouble. It scores deals, flags those with stalled activity or missing stakeholders, and suggests actions. Conversation intelligence summarizes calls and highlights risks, and pipeline inspection tools show where coverage is thin. Revenue leaders use it to prepare for board and forecast meetings.

item.title: Claude
item.description: Claude is the AI assistant from Anthropic, a company that focuses on AI safety research. It comes in a few model tiers, with smaller and faster models for quick tasks and larger ones for harder reasoning and coding. People tend to pick it for writing that sounds less formulaic, careful reading of long documents, and code. It is also more willing than some competitors to say it is unsure or to disagree with you, which some users value and others find less accommodating.

item.title: DataRobot
item.description:
DataRobot pioneered automated machine learning. A data team uploads a dataset, and the platform tries many algorithms and feature combinations, ranks them, and explains the best models, which lowers the barrier to building predictive models for tasks such as churn, demand, and risk. It also handles deployment and monitoring, tracking model accuracy and drift once models are live.

The company has pivoted toward generative AI and agents. Its platform now helps companies build and run AI agents and applications, with governance features such as documentation, bias checks, approvals, and audit trails that matter in industries such as banking, insurance, and healthcare. It can run in the cloud or on a company’s own infrastructure and integrates with major cloud providers and data platforms.

item.title: DocuSign AI
item.description:
Docusign made electronic signatures routine. Senders upload a document, specify signers and fields, and recipients sign on any device, with an audit trail and legal validity in many countries. It’s used for sales contracts, HR paperwork, real estate, and any agreement that once needed a pen, and it integrates with Salesforce, Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, and many business systems.

The company has expanded to manage the whole agreement lifecycle. Its Intelligent Agreement Management platform includes tools to prepare and negotiate agreements, a repository that stores them, and AI that reads contracts to extract terms such as renewal dates, obligations, and parties. Its AI can summarize documents, answer questions about a contract portfolio, and flag risks, and workflow tools automate steps such as approvals and routing.

item.title: Gemini in Workspace
item.description:
Gemini in Workspace brings Google’s models into the apps people use at work. In Gmail, it drafts replies and summarizes long threads. In Docs, it writes, rewrites, and proofreads, and can pull in information from files and email. In Sheets, it helps create formulas, tables, and analysis. In Slides, it generates slides and images, and in Meet it takes notes and summarizes.

A side panel gives a chat assistant that can search across a user’s Drive, Gmail, and Calendar, and answer questions using that content. Organizations can control access, and Google states that business data is not used to train models without permission. Newer features include agents and tools such as NotebookLM for deeper source work.

item.title: Glean
item.description:
Glean addresses the problem that company knowledge lives in dozens of separate tools. It connects to those systems through hundreds of connectors, builds an index of documents, messages, tickets, and other content, and lets employees search across everything from one box. Crucially, it mirrors the permissions of the source systems, so a person only sees results they would already have access to.

On top of search, Glean provides an AI assistant that answers questions in natural language using company information, with citations to the underlying sources. Employees ask things like how a process works, what was decided in a project, or what the latest customer feedback says, and receive a synthesized answer. Glean Agents let teams build automations and agents that take actions in connected apps, and a builder allows non-engineers to create them. Companies can choose among language models from several providers.

item.title: Gong
item.description:
Gong captures sales conversations and turns them into insight. It records calls and meetings, transcribes them, and pulls in emails and CRM data, then analyzes what is happening across the pipeline: which topics come up in deals that close, how often competitors are mentioned, how much reps talk compared with customers, and where deals are stalling. Managers can search a library of calls instead of relying on reps’ summaries.

The AI features save time at several levels. Calls are summarized with key points and next steps, which are written back to the CRM. Deal boards highlight risks, such as no recent contact with a decision-maker, and forecasting tools estimate which deals will close. Coaching tools find moments to review and compare behavior across reps, and newer AI agents help with tasks such as preparing for meetings, researching accounts, and drafting follow-ups.

item.title: Granular
item.description:
Granular was built to help large farm operations plan and track their business. Its software covered field activity and agronomy, inventory, labor, equipment, and financial reporting, and tried to give farm managers a view of costs and profitability for each crop and field. Corteva Agriscience acquired it, and for several years it was marketed to commercial growers who wanted enterprise-level tools.

The product line has since been restructured. Corteva discontinued Granular Agronomy, the field-level software, and sold the financial and business-management side to a company called Traction Ag. The pieces now go by different names and are maintained by different companies, which makes it important to confirm what is currently offered under the Granular name.

item.title: Hootsuite
item.description:
Hootsuite is one of the oldest social media management tools.
