Teams connect accounts for networks such as Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, X, TikTok, and YouTube, plan content on a calendar, schedule posts, and respond to comments and messages in a shared inbox. Approval workflows suit larger organizations.

Listening and analytics tools track brand mentions and compare performance across channels. OwlyWriter, the AI assistant, helps write captions, suggest ideas, and repurpose content. Advertising management and employee advocacy products extend the suite for enterprises.

item.title: HubSpot
item.description: HubSpot started as a marketing software company and grew into a full platform for managing the customer relationship from first visit to renewal. It is organized into hubs: Marketing Hub for email, forms, ads, and landing pages, Sales Hub for pipelines and sequences, Service Hub for tickets and help desk, Content Hub for websites and blogs, and Operations Hub for data syncing and automation. All of them read from the same CRM, so a marketer, a sales rep, and a support agent are looking at one record of the customer.

item.title: HubSpot
item.description: HubSpot began as an inbound marketing tool, and Marketing Hub is still the center of its original idea: attract visitors with useful content, capture them as contacts, and nurture them toward a purchase. It includes email marketing, landing pages, forms, blogging, social publishing, ad tracking, and SEO recommendations, all tied to a CRM that records every interaction with a contact. That shared data is what lets a marketer see which campaigns produce actual customers, not only clicks.

item.title: Jasper
item.description:
For copywriting, Jasper offers more structure than a general chatbot. Marketers choose a format such as a Facebook ad, a product description, a landing page section, or an email sequence, supply the details, and get multiple options in their brand’s voice. The Brand Voice feature learns tone and style from examples, and a company knowledge base provides facts about products and audiences so the copy uses accurate claims.

Collaboration features suit teams. Shared templates and style guides keep writers consistent, and campaigns can be planned in one place with copy, images, and variations for different channels. An editor helps refine text, change tone, and check for plagiarism. Newer agent features help automate common marketing tasks, such as producing a set of assets from a brief.

item.title: Jasper
item.description:
As a marketing platform, Jasper aims to speed up the full path from a brief to a finished campaign. Marketers define their brand voice, audience, and product information once, then generate blog posts, social posts, ads, emails, and landing pages that follow those guidelines. Campaign tools help plan content around a launch, adapt messages for each channel, and keep versions organized.

The latest versions emphasize agents and workflows. Specialized agents handle tasks such as researching a topic, creating a content calendar, repurposing a webinar into several assets, and optimizing copy for search. Integrations connect with tools such as Google Docs, Webflow, and HubSpot, and analytics features tie content to performance. Controls let enterprises govern who can use what and ensure compliance with brand rules.

item.title: Jasper
item.description: Jasper was one of the first dedicated AI writing products and has focused on marketing teams that need a lot of on-brand content. You describe what you need, such as a product launch email or a set of ad variations, and it drafts the copy using your guidelines. Brand Voice learns your tone from sample content, and a knowledge base stores product details, audiences, and approved messaging, so output needs fewer corrections.

item.title: LanguageTool
item.description:
LanguageTool checks writing for spelling, grammar, punctuation, and style, and is notable for its broad language support, including English, German, French, Spanish, Dutch, Portuguese, and many more. It runs as browser extensions, add-ins for Microsoft Word and Google Docs, a desktop app, and an API, so it can check text wherever you write. Many people use it for writing in a second language or switching between languages.

The core engine is open source and can be self-hosted, which appeals to organizations with privacy requirements and to developers who want to integrate a checker. The premium tier adds more advanced style suggestions, tone and clarity feedback, and AI-powered rephrasing, along with higher character limits. Teams can set custom dictionaries and style rules.

item.title: LinkedIn Sales Navigator
item.description:
Sales Navigator gives salespeople deeper access to LinkedIn’s network. It provides advanced filters for finding people and companies, such as by seniority, function, company size, industry, and recent job changes. Users save leads and accounts into lists, and the system sends alerts when something relevant happens, like a prospect changing jobs or a company hiring in a certain department, which can prompt a timely message.

Further features support outreach. InMail messages reach people outside your network, TeamLink shows how colleagues are connected to a prospect for warm introductions, and integrations sync with CRMs such as Salesforce and HubSpot to keep records current. AI tools recommend leads, summarize accounts, and suggest ways to start a conversation, using the profile and activity data on the platform.

item.title: MarketMan
item.description:
MarketMan is back-of-house software for food service. Operators record what they buy and use, build recipes with ingredient costs, and see the cost of each dish. When prices change or usage varies, the system flags it, helping managers protect margins.

Ordering and invoicing are handled in one place. Staff place orders with suppliers, receive deliveries, and match invoices to what arrived, which catches errors and short shipments. Forecasting tools predict how much to order based on sales history, and integrations connect with point of sale and accounting systems.

item.title: MarketMuse
item.description:
MarketMuse approaches content from the perspective of topical authority. It scans your website and compares the topics you cover with what search engines expect from a site in your area, then shows gaps where new or improved content could help. Instead of focusing on single keywords, it helps plan clusters of related articles that together establish expertise.

Its tools turn that strategy into work. Content briefs list the subtopics, questions, and terms a piece should address, an optimization tool scores drafts against those expectations, and AI helps with drafting and updating existing pages. Metrics such as personalized difficulty estimate how hard a topic will be for your site specifically. Teams use the platform to prioritize where to invest effort.

item.title: Moovly
item.description:
Moovly serves companies that need many versions of the same video. Using a template, teams can generate hundreds or thousands of variations that change names, products, languages, or data, such as personalized sales videos or product videos for each item in a catalog. A browser editor handles design, and an API automates production from spreadsheets or other systems.

Localization is a major theme. Moovly can add subtitles, translate scripts, and generate voiceovers in multiple languages using AI voices, helping companies serve international audiences, and AI tools assist with text-to-video and editing. It’s used in marketing, e-commerce, training, and communications, and offers brand controls and collaboration for large teams.

item.title: Netomi
item.description:
Netomi builds AI agents for customer support. Large brands connect it to their help desks and back-end systems, and the agents answer questions, track orders, process returns, and handle other requests across channels. Where an agent cannot resolve something, it hands off to a person with context.

The platform learns from past tickets and company content, and is built with controls such as guardrails and testing for regulated and high-volume environments. Customers include airlines, retailers, and travel companies that field heavy, repetitive inquiries.

item.title: Nintex
item.description:
Nintex helps organizations digitize their processes. Using a visual designer, business analysts build workflows that route requests, collect approvals, update systems, and send notifications, and they create forms to start those workflows. It integrates with Microsoft 365, SharePoint, Salesforce, and many other systems, which is where its roots lie, with many customers automating processes on SharePoint.

The platform has several parts. Process mapping tools document how work actually happens, automation tools execute workflows and robotic process automation, and document generation tools produce contracts and reports from data. AI features assist with building workflows from descriptions and extracting data from documents, and analytics show where processes slow down.

item.title: Oracle SCM
item.description:
Oracle SCM Cloud brings the functions of a supply chain together in one cloud application suite. It covers planning demand and supply, buying from suppliers, managing inventory and warehouses, running manufacturing, handling orders and fulfillment, and moving goods through transportation and global trade, with product lifecycle management for design data. Because it shares data with Oracle’s finance and HR applications, companies can connect supply chain decisions to financial outcomes.

AI and analytics support the suite. Machine learning improves demand forecasts and supply plans, predictive models flag delays and quality risks, and generative AI assistants help users find information and complete tasks. Oracle has been adding AI agents that can handle routine actions across processes. The suite is delivered in the cloud and updated regularly.

item.title: Outreach
item.description:
Outreach is used by sales teams to run structured prospecting and follow-up at scale. Reps enroll leads in sequences that combine emails, calls, LinkedIn steps, and tasks, and the platform schedules each step, tracks replies, and logs activity to the CRM. Managers can see which messages and cadences perform best, and automated rules route leads and keep work organized.

Over time, Outreach has added revenue intelligence and AI. Conversation intelligence records and analyzes calls, deal health scoring flags risk, and forecasting tools combine activity and pipeline data to estimate outcomes. AI assistants summarize meetings, draft emails, suggest next steps, and increasingly act as agents that research accounts or manage parts of the pipeline.

item.title: PandaDoc AI
item.description:
PandaDoc helps sales teams close deals faster. Users build proposals and quotes from templates in a drag-and-drop editor, add pricing tables with live calculations, embed videos and payment links, and send them to clients, who can review and sign electronically. Tracking shows when a document is opened and viewed, so reps know when to follow up.

Automation and integration make it practical for teams. It connects with CRMs like Salesforce and HubSpot to populate documents with deal data and update records when documents are signed, offers approval workflows, content libraries, and a payment step. AI features help generate document content from a prompt, summarize contracts, suggest edits, and extract information, speeding up proposal creation.

item.title: People.ai
item.description:
People.ai solves the data entry problem in sales. Instead of relying on reps to log everything, it connects to email, calendars, and phone systems and records contacts, meetings, and conversations, then matches them to the right accounts and opportunities in the CRM. That keeps records current and gives managers a more complete picture of how engaged each deal is.

On top of the data, it provides analytics and AI. Dashboards show activity, engagement with key contacts, and whether deals are at risk, and forecasting tools estimate which will close. AI agents can summarize accounts, answer questions about the pipeline in natural language, and prepare reps for meetings. The aim is to give sales leaders a reliable view without chasing updates.

item.title: Persado
item.description:
Persado focuses on the specific words in marketing messages. Its premise is that the choice of language, including emotions, calls to action, and phrasing, affects whether people respond, and that machine learning can learn what works. Marketers give it a campaign goal and brand guidelines, and it generates message variations and predicts which will perform best, based on its library of language and results from past campaigns.

Large brands in finance, retail, and telecommunications use Persado to optimize email subject lines, ads, and push notifications at scale. It integrates with marketing platforms, tests variants, and learns from the results to improve future messages. More recently, the company has added generative AI tools for drafting and personalizing content within brand guardrails.

item.title: Phrase
item.description:
Phrase helps companies translate software and content into many languages. Developers connect repositories and design tools, and new text is sent to translators or machine translation, then returned to the product when approved. Translation memory reuses earlier work and glossaries keep terminology consistent.

The platform brings together several products that grew from a merger: a translation management system, a string management tool for software teams, and a computer-assisted translation editor. AI translation engines and quality estimation reduce the amount of human review needed for lower-risk content.

item.title: Pinecone
item.description:
Pinecone provides the storage and search layer for applications that work with embeddings, which are numerical representations of text, images, or other data. A developer converts documents into vectors, stores them in Pinecone, and later retrieves the ones closest in meaning to a query. That pattern powers retrieval-augmented generation, where a language model answers using relevant stored passages, as well as semantic search and recommendation systems.

The service is fully managed and serverless, so developers don’t provision servers or manage indexes by hand, and it scales with usage. It supports metadata filtering, hybrid search that combines keyword and semantic methods, namespaces to separate data, and tools for generating embeddings and reranking results. Pinecone also offers an assistant product that handles document chat with minimal setup, and integrations with LangChain, LlamaIndex, and the major model providers.

item.title: Privy
item.description:
Privy gives small stores a way to capture and convert visitors. Pop-ups and banners collect emails and texts with offers, automated emails recover abandoned carts, and campaigns promote products to subscribers. Everything runs from one dashboard connected to the store.

AI assists with writing and targeting, such as drafting emails and choosing segments. Templates and recipes simplify setup for merchants without a marketing team, and analytics show revenue from each campaign.

item.title: Proposify
item.description:
Proposify helps agencies and service companies create and send proposals. Teams build templates with sections, pricing tables, and brand styling, assemble a proposal quickly, and send it to clients who can review, comment, and sign electronically. Notifications show when a proposal is opened.

AI features help with writing content and suggest improvements based on what has worked in past proposals. Analytics reveal how long clients spend on each section, informing follow-ups. Integrations connect with CRMs and billing.

item.title: Qwilr
item.description:
Qwilr replaces static PDF proposals with web pages. A seller builds a proposal from blocks, such as text, images, videos, pricing tables, and acceptance sections, and sends a link. Buyers can adjust options in a pricing table, and sign online, which shortens the path to closing.

Analytics show who viewed the page, how long they spent on each section, and when they came back, which guides follow-up. Templates keep branding consistent, and integrations push data into CRMs. AI drafts content from notes and suggests improvements.

item.title: Salesforce
item.description: Salesforce is the CRM that large companies tend to run their sales and customer operations on. It tracks leads, accounts, opportunities, and support cases, and it is sold as separate clouds for Sales, Service, Marketing, and Commerce, with Slack, Tableau, and MuleSoft added for collaboration, analytics, and integration. Underneath is a platform that lets companies build custom objects, workflows, and apps, which is why Salesforce setups can look very different from one company to the next.

item.title: Salesforce Einstein
item.description:
Einstein brought AI to Salesforce customers well before generative AI became popular. Predictive features score leads and opportunities, forecast revenue, recommend next best actions, and flag at-risk accounts, using each company’s own CRM data. Einstein Discovery finds patterns and suggests what drives outcomes, and bots and analytics features extend the same ideas to service and marketing.

With generative AI, Einstein has expanded to write emails, summarize records and cases, and generate service replies, grounded in customer data and protected by the Einstein Trust Layer, which masks sensitive information and prevents customer data from being used to train outside models. The conversational assistant evolved into Agentforce, which builds autonomous agents on the same foundation, so Einstein now refers to a mix of older predictive features and the generative AI infrastructure.

item.title: SalesLoft
item.description:
Salesloft helps sales teams organize outbound and follow-up work. Reps follow cadences, which are structured sequences of emails, calls, and social touches, and the platform tells them who to contact next and records each activity in the CRM. Managers can see which messages and sequences generate replies and meetings, and coach reps with call recordings and analytics.

The platform has expanded into revenue orchestration. Conversation intelligence records and summarizes calls, deal management tracks stage progress and risk, and forecasting tools combine pipeline data with engagement signals. Salesloft acquired Drift for conversational marketing and has combined with Clari, a revenue forecasting company, to build a broader revenue platform. AI assistants prepare meeting briefs, draft messages, and suggest next steps.

item.title: SAP Ariba
item.description:
SAP Ariba helps large organizations buy what they need in an organized way. Procurement teams use it to find and evaluate suppliers, run sourcing events, manage contracts, process purchase orders and invoices, and monitor supplier risk. The Ariba Network connects buyers and suppliers electronically, so orders and invoices flow between systems without manual entry.

AI is being added to reduce manual work. SAP’s assistant, Joule, can help users search for information, draft sourcing documents, and answer questions about spend, and features analyze contracts, recommend suppliers, and flag unusual transactions. Integration with SAP’s ERP and other systems provides a connected view of purchasing, and spend analytics reveal savings opportunities.

item.title: Scale AI
item.description:
Scale AI built its business on a simple observation: AI models need huge amounts of well-labeled data, and quality control at scale is hard. It combines software with a large network of human contributors and experts to annotate images, video, text, and sensor data. Early customers included self-driving car developers, and the company grew by supplying training data to the biggest AI labs.

Today much of its work involves large language models. Scale provides human feedback data used in reinforcement learning, expert-written examples for fine-tuning, and evaluations that test models for accuracy and safety. Its tools help companies manage data pipelines, and a generative AI platform lets enterprises customize models on their own data. Public-sector work includes AI systems for defense and government agencies, and the company runs public leaderboards that rank models on hard tests.

item.title: Sembly AI
item.description:
Sembly joins your online meetings, records them, and produces a transcript with a structured summary. The summary highlights the main points, tasks, decisions, and risks mentioned, so teams can see what needs follow-up without rewatching. It also supports in-person meetings through its mobile app and uploads of audio files, and works in many languages.

Beyond single meetings, Sembly helps organize knowledge. Workspaces and meeting libraries let teams search past conversations and ask questions across them, and templates adjust the notes for different meeting types such as sales calls or interviews. Integrations push summaries and tasks into Slack, Notion, Asana, Jira, HubSpot, and other tools. Analytics track patterns like meeting time and topics.

item.title: ServiceNow
item.description:
ServiceNow began as an IT service management tool and became a general workflow platform for large organizations. Employees and customers submit requests, such as a laptop problem, a payroll question, or a customer complaint, and the platform routes, tracks, and resolves them using defined workflows. Companies use it as a system of record and action across IT operations, HR, legal, security, and customer service.

AI is central to its current strategy. Now Assist adds generative AI to summarize cases, draft replies, and help agents find answers, and AI agents can take on tasks such as triaging incidents and fulfilling requests with minimal human intervention. The company acquired Moveworks, whose employee assistant is intended to become the front door to the platform, and offers tools to govern and monitor agents across the enterprise.

item.title: Shopify
item.description: Shopify lets someone start an online store without building the software behind it. You choose a theme, add products, set up payments and shipping, and the platform handles hosting, the checkout, and tax and currency settings. The same system also covers in-person sales through point-of-sale hardware, so a shop can manage online and physical inventory together. Everything from a one-person side business to large brands runs on it, and Shop Pay, its accelerated checkout, is used well beyond Shopify’s own stores.

item.title: SimilarWeb
item.description:
Similarweb lets you look at the performance of sites you do not own. Enter a domain, and it shows estimated monthly visits, traffic sources such as search, social, and direct, top keywords, referring sites, audience demographics, and engagement metrics like time on site. Data comes from a mix of panels, partnerships, and public sources, modeled to produce estimates. This helps in benchmarking competitors and finding growth opportunities.

The platform covers more than websites. It tracks app usage and downloads, advertising, and market segments, and ranks sites within categories. Recent additions include tracking how brands and sites are cited and visited through AI chatbots, reflecting the way people increasingly use AI assistants instead of search. Investors use the data to spot trends in company performance before financial reports, and sales teams use it to find leads.

item.title: simpleshow
item.description:
simpleshow is known for its hand-drawn, paper-cutout explainer style. A user pastes a script or topic, and the engine suggests images and structure, generates a video with narration, and lets the user edit scenes. The goal is to make complex subjects clear for training and communications.

Companies use it for onboarding, compliance, product explanations, and internal updates. The platform is aimed at non-designers and provides templates and a library of illustrations.

item.title: Smartcat
item.description:
Smartcat brings machine and human translation together. A company uploads documents or connects content sources, receives AI translation immediately, and can request human review from freelance linguists or agencies in its marketplace, all with translation memory and glossaries.

Workflow tools manage projects, deadlines, and payments, and the platform supports many file types and integrations. AI agents handle tasks such as quality checks, and the pricing model aims to keep costs lower than traditional agencies.

item.title: Sourcegraph Cody
item.description: Cody grew out of Sourcegraph’s code search, which indexes entire repositories and lets developers find and understand code across many projects. That context was its main advantage: instead of guessing from the open file, Cody could draw on the broader codebase to answer questions, write code that matched existing patterns, and explain how parts of a system fit together. It worked in VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, and the web, with chat, autocomplete, and commands to edit and test code.

item.title: Sprout Social
item.description:
Sprout Social is built for teams that manage social media as a function, not a side task. A calendar plans and schedules content across networks such as Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, X, and TikTok, and approval flows keep drafts under review before they go out. A smart inbox gathers messages, comments, and mentions from every channel into one stream that can be assigned, tagged, and replied to by a team.

Analytics are a major selling point. Reports show how posts perform, how audiences grow, and how competitors compare, and they can be exported or shared with clients and executives. Listening tools track brand mentions, topics, and sentiment across social and the web, which helps with crisis monitoring and market research. Influencer marketing and employee advocacy tools extend into related work. AI Assist helps write posts, change tone, and draft replies, and it can summarize sentiment from conversations.

item.title: Square
item.description:
Square is known for its card readers and registers. A small business accepts payments in person, online, or by invoice, tracks inventory, and manages staff and payroll from a single account. Hardware ranges from a simple reader to full countertop systems.

Additional services include appointments, loyalty programs, marketing, and small business loans based on sales. AI assistance writes item descriptions, generates insights from sales data, and answers business questions.

Square charges processing fees per transaction and sells hardware, with paid software tiers for advanced features. It has a free plan for basic use. Alternatives include Toast for restaurants, Clover, Shopify POS, Stripe Terminal, and SumUp. Square suits small retail and food businesses.

item.title: Synthesia
item.description:
Synthesia produces videos with digital presenters. Users select from a library of avatars or create a custom one, paste a script, choose a voice and language, and receive a finished video. The editor handles slides, text, and media.

Companies use it for training, onboarding, product explainers, and communications, often replacing costly shoots. Translations let one video serve many markets. Recent features add interactive videos, screen recording, and avatars with more expressive delivery.

item.title: Synthesia
item.description:
Synthesia lets companies produce videos without cameras, studios, or actors. A user writes or pastes a script, selects an AI avatar from a library of presenters or creates a custom one, and the platform generates a video with natural speech and lip movement. Scenes, slides, screen recordings, and media can be combined, and editing the script and regenerating takes the place of a reshoot.

The platform is built for business use. It supports a large number of languages, so one video can be localized quickly, and offers templates, brand kits, and collaboration features. Interactive and agent-style avatars can respond to viewers, and an API lets teams automate video creation. Enterprise features cover security, compliance, and consent controls, since custom avatars require permission from the person depicted. Companies commonly use it for learning and development, onboarding, product explainers, and sales content.

item.title: Tabnine
item.description:
Tabnine was one of the earliest AI code completion tools, and it built its identity on privacy and control. It works inside VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, and other editors, suggesting lines and functions, answering questions in chat, writing tests and documentation, and explaining code. A distinguishing choice was letting companies run it in their own environment, including fully disconnected networks, and keeping code out of any third party’s training.

Its enterprise pitch centers on context. Tabnine can learn from a company’s repositories, style guides, and standards so suggestions match internal conventions, and administrators can choose which models are used, including options hosted in-house. It offers attribution and provenance controls for companies worried about generated code resembling open-source projects with restrictive licenses. Agents extend it to larger tasks such as code review and test generation.

item.title: Toast
item.description:
Toast serves the restaurant industry. Servers take orders on handheld devices, kitchen displays route tickets, guests pay at the table or online, and managers track sales, labor, and inventory. Online ordering, delivery integrations, and loyalty programs are part of the ecosystem.

Data and AI support operations. Sales forecasts help schedule staff, menu analytics show what sells, and assistants help write menu descriptions and answer business questions. Payroll and team management tools extend the suite.

item.title: Tray.io
item.description:
Tray.io builds on the idea of integration-platform-as-a-service. Teams use a visual builder to create workflows that connect SaaS applications, databases, and internal systems, with powerful logic, error handling, and the ability to write code where necessary. Hundreds of connectors and a universal connector for APIs cover common enterprise tools such as Salesforce, Workday, and Slack.

The company has moved toward AI agents. Its Merlin AI tools let teams build agents that use the connected systems as tools, so an agent can look up a customer, update a record, and send a message, with governance over what it can access. Embedded integration products let software companies offer customer-facing integrations in their own products.

item.title: UiPath
item.description:
UiPath popularized robotic process automation, in which software robots mimic what a person does on a screen. Developers build automations in a studio by recording and arranging steps such as clicking, copying data between systems, and filling forms, and run them on servers or desktops. This is valuable for companies with legacy systems that lack APIs, since bots can work through the same interfaces people use.

The platform has expanded into AI. Document understanding extracts data from invoices and forms, process mining reveals which workflows are worth automating, and agent tools let AI agents plan and carry out tasks, orchestrated alongside robots and people. The Maestro orchestration layer coordinates agents, robots, and human steps, and governance features control access and auditing.

item.title: Vertex AI
item.description: Vertex AI is where Google Cloud customers build with AI. At its center is Model Garden, a catalog that includes Google’s Gemini, Imagen, and Veo models, open models like Llama and Gemma, and models from partners such as Anthropic. You can call a model through an API, test it in a studio, and then deploy it with Google Cloud’s security, networking, and compliance controls. Data stays under the customer’s governance, which matters for regulated industries.

item.title: Watershed
item.description:
Watershed focuses on carbon accounting for large companies. Organizations connect data from finance systems, energy bills, travel, and suppliers, and the platform converts that activity data into greenhouse gas emissions across all scopes, including the harder-to-measure supply chain. The methods follow recognized standards and are designed to stand up to audits, which matters as more companies face disclosure rules.

Beyond measurement, the platform supports action. Companies set targets, model reduction scenarios, and track progress, and tools for engaging suppliers help gather better data and cut emissions in the value chain. Reporting features produce disclosures for frameworks and regulations, and AI helps classify purchases, fill gaps in data, and prepare reports, which reduces the manual effort that carbon accounting requires.

item.title: Webflow
item.description:
Webflow sits between simple site builders and hand-coded sites. Designers work on a canvas that mirrors how the web works, setting classes, flexbox and grid layouts, and breakpoints, and the platform produces production code and hosts the result. That gives far more control than template-based builders, which is why agencies and in-house design teams like it.

The platform includes a CMS for blogs and collections, e-commerce, interactions and animations, localization, and tools for marketers to edit content without breaking the design. AI features generate sections and copy, suggest changes, and help with site structure and SEO. Developers can add custom code and use an API to connect Webflow to other services.

item.title: WellSaid Labs
item.description:
WellSaid focuses on voiceovers for businesses. In its web studio, you type or paste a script, pick a voice, and generate narration with control over pacing, pronunciation, and emphasis. The voices are built from recordings by professional voice actors who agreed to the use, which gives companies a clear license position. Typical projects include training courses, explainer videos, product tours, corporate announcements, and audio for apps.

For larger teams, collaboration and control matter. Projects can be shared, commented on, and reviewed, and custom pronunciation settings keep brand names and technical terms consistent across a library of content. An API lets developers add speech to their own products, and integrations connect WellSaid to e-learning and creative tools. Enterprise plans emphasize security, privacy, and compliance, and custom voices can be created for a brand.

item.title: Workato
item.description:
Workato is an integration and automation platform. Teams build recipes that link applications such as Salesforce, Workday, and Slack, trigger actions, and move data. Business users can create simple automations while IT governs the platform.

The company has added AI across the product. Users describe a workflow in plain language and Workato builds a draft, document understanding extracts data, and agents handle tasks with enterprise controls. Governance, security, and monitoring suit regulated companies.

item.title: Workday
item.description:
Workday began as cloud HR software and expanded into financials. Large employers use it to keep employee records, run payroll and benefits, manage recruiting and performance, plan headcount and budgets, and close the books. Having HR and finance on one data model helps companies tie workforce decisions to costs.

AI shows up across the suite. It suggests candidates and skills matches, flags attrition risks, helps managers with planning, and drafts job descriptions and summaries. Workday has also introduced AI agents that take on tasks inside its apps, along with an agent management layer so that companies can control what those agents may do. It has bought AI companies to extend this, including some that build agent platforms.

item.title: Writerly
item.description:
Writerly is aimed at teams that want AI-written content to sound like them. Instead of generating generic text, it lets users supply samples of their existing writing and style guidelines, then drafts articles, emails, and social posts that follow that voice. That approach is common among brand-focused writing tools, and matters most for companies with several writers.

Features reported in directories include templates for common content types, collaboration for editors and reviewers, and options to reuse past content. Teams often use this kind of tool to keep messaging consistent across channels and to speed up first drafts, with humans editing for accuracy and judgment.

item.title: Zoho
item.description:
Zoho builds a wide range of business applications on its own platform. Companies can use Zoho CRM for sales, Books for accounting, Desk for support, Projects for work tracking, Mail for email, People for HR, and dozens of other apps, many of which integrate with one another. Zoho One bundles the whole suite for a single per-user price.

Zia is the AI layer. It predicts which leads are likely to convert, detects anomalies in data, drafts replies, and answers questions in natural language, and Zoho has added a generative assistant and agents that can act across apps. The company also supports the option of running models on its own infrastructure for customers who want data kept in their region.

item.title: ZoomInfo
item.description:
ZoomInfo provides one of the largest databases of business contacts and companies. Sales and marketing teams search by title, industry, company size, location, and technology to build lists, and see verified email addresses, direct phone numbers, org charts, and firmographic details. Intent data shows which companies are researching topics related to a product, helping teams reach out when interest is high.

The platform has expanded from data into a workflow product. It includes tools for sales engagement, marketing advertising, conversation intelligence through Chorus, and enrichment that keeps CRM records up to date automatically. AI features include assistants that research accounts, draft outreach, and recommend who to contact, and agents that handle prospecting tasks. It integrates with Salesforce, HubSpot, and other systems.

item.title: ABBYY
item.description:
ABBYY has worked with optical character recognition for decades. Its FineReader software converts scanned pages and PDFs into editable text, and its enterprise products read invoices, contracts, IDs, and forms at scale. Machine learning classifies the type of document, locates key fields such as invoice totals and dates, and extracts the data in a structured form that other systems can use.

The platform has expanded into intelligent document processing. Pre-trained skills handle common document types without training, while companies can build custom models for their own forms. Validation tools route low-confidence results to human review, and integrations connect with robotic process automation, ERP, and content management systems. ABBYY has added generative AI features and tools for making documents ready for use by language models, as companies seek to feed documents into AI workflows.

item.title: Aisera
item.description: Aisera provides AI agents for internal and external service desks. Employees can ask for help with IT issues, such as resetting a password or requesting software, or HR questions, such as time off policies, and the agent resolves the request by taking actions in connected systems instead of simply pointing to articles. For customers, similar agents handle support inquiries. The goal is to reduce the number of tickets that reach human staff.

item.title: Beamery
item.description:
Beamery treats talent like a relationship, not a one-off hire. Recruiters build pools of potential candidates, track interactions, run campaigns to stay in touch, and see who might fit upcoming roles. The same system can surface current employees for internal moves, which helps companies fill jobs from within.

Its AI builds around skills. It infers skills from resumes and profiles, maps them to a company’s roles, and recommends matches for jobs and development. Workforce planning tools help leaders see skill gaps and plan hiring or training. Integrations connect with applicant tracking systems such as Workday and SuccessFactors.

item.title: Coupa
item.description:
Coupa gives companies control over what they spend. Employees request purchases through approved channels, procurement manages suppliers and contracts, and accounts payable processes invoices and payments. Having it in one system improves visibility and helps enforce policy.

The company’s distinctive asset is aggregated data. With permission, Coupa analyzes anonymized spend across its customer base to benchmark prices, identify supplier risk, and recommend savings. AI features help with spend classification, contract review, and answering questions about spending, and supplier networks connect buyers with vendors.

item.title: Diffbot
item.description:
Diffbot uses computer vision and natural language processing to read web pages the way a person would. Instead of writing a scraper for each site, developers send a URL to its APIs and receive structured data about articles, products, or people, regardless of page layout.

The company also built a large knowledge graph, a database of entities such as organizations, people, and products, with relationships collected from across the web. Customers query it to enrich records, monitor news, find companies matching criteria, or give language models grounded facts. Its extraction tools support crawling at scale.

item.title: HyperScience
item.description:
HyperScience automates paperwork-heavy processes. Organizations in insurance, banking, and government feed forms, letters, and claims into the platform, which classifies each document, extracts fields, and passes clean data to downstream systems. Handwriting recognition covers documents that older tools struggled with.

A human-in-the-loop design handles low-confidence results: reviewers check flagged fields, and their corrections improve the models. The platform has added large language model features for understanding unstructured text and answering questions about documents, and it supports on-premises and private cloud deployment for sensitive data.

item.title: Kinaxis
item.description:
Kinaxis helps large manufacturers and retailers plan and respond. Its platform brings demand, supply, inventory, and capacity into one model that updates together, rather than in separate steps, so planners can test the effect of a disruption or a decision in minutes.

Planners run what-if scenarios, see the impact on service and cost, and collaborate across functions. Machine learning improves demand sensing and supply risk detection, and newer AI agents help summarize issues and recommend actions. Customers include companies in high tech, life sciences, automotive, and consumer goods.

item.title: Reka AI
item.description:
Reka is a research lab and company founded by researchers from DeepMind, Google, and Meta. It trains models from scratch that take mixed inputs, so a user can ask questions about a video or combine audio and text. The Flash and Edge models are smaller and faster, and Core is the largest.

Products built on the models include tools for research tasks that search and reason over the web, and for analyzing video. Developers use the API, and the company has released some models openly. Efficiency is a recurring theme in its work.

item.title: SmartRecruiters
item.description:
SmartRecruiters is an applicant tracking system built for large companies. Recruiters post jobs to many boards, receive and manage applications, collaborate with hiring managers on evaluations, schedule interviews, and extend offers, all in one workflow. A marketplace of integrations connects background checks, assessments, video interviewing, and HR systems, which suits global companies with complex hiring needs.

AI features support sourcing and screening. The platform recommends candidates from existing applicants and external pools, scores fit against job requirements, and helps with scheduling and communication. Its AI assistant can draft job descriptions and summarize candidate profiles, and analytics show the hiring funnel, time to fill, and diversity metrics. The company states it emphasizes transparency in how AI recommendations are made.

item.title: Speechmatics
item.description:
Speechmatics provides speech-to-text as a service. Developers send audio and get transcripts with timestamps, speaker labels, and language detection. The company emphasizes accuracy across accents and dialects, which is an area where many systems show bias.

Products include real-time transcription for live captioning and voice agents, batch processing, translation, and deployment options on premises for sensitive data. Customers include media, contact center, and healthcare companies.

Speechmatics is priced by usage. Alternatives include Deepgram, AssemblyAI, OpenAI Whisper, Gladia, and Google Cloud Speech-to-Text. Speechmatics suits organizations needing accurate multilingual transcription.

item.title: Trint
item.description:
Trint speeds up working with recordings. Users upload interviews, press conferences, or footage and get transcripts that link to the audio, so editing the text is easy to verify. Teams can search across an archive, highlight quotes, and build stories from selections.

The platform supports many languages, translation, and subtitles, and offers collaboration for newsrooms with permissions and shared workspaces. AI features create summaries and help extract key moments.

Trint is paid, with plans by features and seats. Accuracy depends on audio quality. Alternatives include Otter.ai, Descript, Transkriptor, Verbit, and Rev. Trint suits media teams that work with large volumes of recorded content.

item.title: Vectara
item.description:
Vectara offers RAG as a service. Developers upload documents or connect sources, and the platform handles chunking, embedding, retrieval, and generation, returning answers with citations. Teams avoid assembling these components themselves.

The company emphasizes factual consistency, publishing a hallucination evaluation model and leaderboard, and offers agent features. Security options include private deployments for sensitive data.

Vectara has a free tier and paid plans by usage. Retrieval quality still depends on document quality. Alternatives include Pinecone with custom pipelines, Cohere, Azure AI Search, Glean, and LlamaIndex. Vectara suits teams that want RAG without building infrastructure.

item.title: Verbit
item.description:
Verbit blends machine and human work. AI produces a first draft of the transcript, and professional editors review and correct it, which yields higher accuracy than automatic transcription alone. Services include captioning for live events, court reporting, and transcripts of recorded media.

Education is a big market: universities use Verbit to caption lectures and meet accessibility requirements. Its platform integrates with video tools and learning systems, and the company has acquired several transcription and captioning firms.

item.title: Clearscope
item.description: Clearscope helps writers produce content that is complete enough to rank. You enter a keyword, and it analyzes the top results to show the terms, topics, and questions that strong pages tend to include. As you draft in its editor, a grade updates, so you can see whether the page covers what searchers expect. Plugins for Google Docs, Word, and WordPress let writers work in familiar tools instead of switching to a separate app.

item.title: Cohere
item.description:
Cohere sells AI to businesses and keeps its focus there. Its flagship Command models handle generation, summarization, and tool use, while Embed turns text into vectors for semantic search, and Rerank reorders search results by relevance. Together those pieces form the backbone of retrieval-augmented generation, where a model answers from a company’s own documents instead of from memory. Cohere also builds models for translation, document parsing, and speech transcription.

What differentiates it from OpenAI and Anthropic is how it is deployed. Cohere models can run on major clouds, in a customer’s private cloud, or fully on-premises, which suits banks, governments, and healthcare organizations that cannot send data to a public service. North is its workplace platform for AI agents that search company data and complete tasks, and Compass provides enterprise search. The company’s research arm also releases open-weight models for non-commercial use.

item.title: Competitor Analyzer
item.description:
Competitor Analyzer helps small teams keep an eye on the market without a full-time analyst. You enter your competitors, and the tool watches their websites, social accounts, content, and in some cases pricing, then summarizes what changed in a weekly digest. The aim is to save the time spent checking sites by hand.

Typical uses include spotting a rival’s new feature or campaign, tracking pricing changes, and gathering material for positioning. AI summaries make the digests quick to read and highlight notable changes. The tool is positioned as simpler and cheaper than enterprise competitive intelligence platforms.

item.title: Denovo
item.description:
Denovo aims to shorten the path from idea to launched business. A user describes what they want to start, and the platform helps produce a business plan, suggests names and branding, generates a website, and walks through setup tasks such as registering the company. Putting these steps in one tool reduces the number of services a beginner must find and learn.

The target is people who have never started a company, or who want to test a side project quickly. AI-generated plans and sites provide a starting point, and users still need to validate demand with real customers and check legal requirements in their location.

item.title: Eightfold AI
item.description:
Eightfold AI treats talent as a graph of skills. Its models read resumes, job descriptions, and employee profiles, infer skills, and match people to roles based on what they can do and are likely to learn, not just on keywords or job titles. Recruiters use it to find candidates in a company’s applicant database and external sources, and employees can see roles and learning paths that fit their skills.

The platform extends across the employee lifecycle. Modules cover talent acquisition, talent management, internal mobility, and workforce planning, with analytics that show skill gaps and diversity trends. Agent-style features automate steps such as screening and scheduling. It integrates with applicant tracking and HR systems such as Workday and SAP SuccessFactors.

item.title: HireVue
item.description:
HireVue lets candidates complete interviews on their own schedule. Employers set up structured questions, candidates record video answers, and recruiters review them later, which saves scheduling time when hiring many people. The platform has expanded to include game-based and skills assessments, live interviews, text-based chat for scheduling and screening, and tools for coding interviews.

Its use of AI has been controversial. HireVue once analyzed facial expressions and voice in interviews, which drew criticism from privacy and civil rights groups, and it dropped facial analysis. Today it describes using structured scoring based on what candidates say and on job-relevant skills, and publishes audits and explanations of its models. Regulations in places such as New York City and Illinois now require notice, consent, or bias audits for automated hiring tools.

item.title: Iris.ai
item.description: Iris.ai aims to reduce the time scientists spend finding and reading relevant papers. Instead of keyword searches, a researcher can input a problem description or an abstract, and the system finds related papers by meaning. It then helps explore the results with a visual map of topics, filters based on content, and tools that extract data and summarize findings across many documents. Research teams use it to scan a field, check for prior work, and decide where to focus.

item.title: Komos
item.description:
Komos aims to replace fragile recorded scripts with instructions in natural language. A user describes a task, such as downloading reports from a portal or entering data across systems, and an AI agent carries it out by operating a browser, adjusting when a page changes.

That approach targets a known weakness of traditional robotic process automation, where small interface changes break bots. Enterprise teams use such tools for back-office tasks in systems that lack APIs.

item.title: LlamaIndex
item.description: LlamaIndex started as an open-source library for connecting language models to private data, and that remains its core job. It helps load information from files, databases, APIs, and apps such as Notion and Slack, split it into pieces, index it, and retrieve the relevant parts when a user asks a question. This retrieval-augmented generation pattern is how many company chatbots answer from internal documents instead of from the model’s general knowledge.

item.title: Slack AI
item.description:
Slack AI addresses the problem of catching up. When you return from time off or join a busy channel, it can summarize what happened, list decisions, and highlight what needs your attention. Thread summaries cut long discussions into a few lines, and daily recaps cover channels you choose, so you can stay informed without reading every message.

AI search turns Slack into a place to ask questions. Instead of hunting for keywords, you can ask something like what the timeline is for a project, and receive an answer drawn from messages, files, and connected apps, with links to the sources. Slackbot is being reshaped as an assistant that can help draft messages, find information, and take actions, and Salesforce’s Agentforce agents can work in Slack. Huddle notes summarize audio calls.

item.title: Tidio
item.description:
Tidio targets small online businesses that want to answer customers quickly without a big support team. A chat widget on the website lets visitors ask questions, and the tool collects messages from chat, email, and social channels in one inbox. Visual chatbot flows handle common tasks, such as collecting contact details, recommending products, and recovering abandoned carts.

Lyro, its AI agent, answers customer questions using the store’s help content and product data, and hands off to a human when needed. Automations trigger messages based on visitor behavior, and integrations with Shopify, WordPress, WooCommerce, and others bring in order and product information. Tidio is aimed at ease of setup, and most stores can install it in minutes.
